answer.rationale: The 18% spend cut and 14-day renewal deadline create urgency, but the assembly line's 94% utilization leaves no margin for sourcing misstep. Memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments with the incumbent unlocked volume pricing; memory_c4 demonstrates that renegotiation at renewal can recover real margin and move the incumbent on price and payment terms. Memory_c2 shows switching cut unit cost sharply, but switching now risks onboarding friction with zero buffer. Verifying memory_c4 confirms whether benchmarking-driven renegotiation is repeatable at this cycle. Negotiating terms with the incumbent offers the highest probability of achieving the 18% target while preserving delivery stability—the incumbent knows our volume, integration is proven, and renegotiation has succeeded before. This avoids the execution risk of a switch (onboarding under deadline) and the cost of adding a second source when we need immediate savings. Deferring is not viable given the 14-day expiration and non-auto-renewal clause. A standard experiment scope allows negotiation to play out without locking in a multi-year commitment until terms are proven acceptable.
